cue: Hold still, as a spider holds its web. Only what moves reaches you.
rows: A Golden Silk Spider feels its prey through the silk, and a trapped insect shakes the web 5 to 30 times a second. The shaking arrives ten to thirty times stronger on some legs than on others, which gives the direction.
Most spiders have eight eyes and few see well. Most register little more than changes between light and dark, and spiders that build webs lean on the shaking of the silk.
A wandering spider resolves nothing finer than about 2 degrees, under a hundredth of your sharpness. The picture borrows that figure for web builders.
A wandering spider stops following flicker between 4.3 and 8.6 times a second, a seventh of your rate or less, so movement smears into trails.

Where the phone’s motion sensors or its microphone are switched on, a knock on the phone or on the table it lies on, or a low sound, sends ripples across the picture. They stand in for a shaking web, and the ripples are the app’s own drawing.
A bridge spider turns toward a loudspeaker three metres away, because its web moves with the air and works as a listening surface up to 10,000 times larger than its body.
Wolf spiders have four large rear eyes backed by a mirror layer, which shines back in a flashlight beam and helps them spot movement in dim light. This picture leaves that out.

With &draw=web the picture carries a drawn web that shakes and flashes with knocks and sounds. With &draw=air, breath on the microphone ruffles the picture. With &draw=buzz the phone buzzes at a knock. Each drawing is the app's.

rows.title: Eyes
rows.text: Most spiders have eight eyes, and you very likely have eight as well. Only a few families, among them the recluse spiders, the woodlouse hunters and the goblin spiders, have six, and they lack the middle pair at the front.
rows.note: Land 1985: six eyes in Sicariidae, Dysderidae and Oonopidae, with the principal eyes missing. The claim about what the side eyes do is left out, since the sources hedge it. Graded g, as live: the count rests on an order-level record; rows.py computes i because no species of the view is measured.
rows.rewrite_reason: Draft uses Latin family names (recluse and goblin spiders), hedges ('regarded as'), and overstates that nobody has measured how your eyes are built.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: Nobody has measured how sharply you see. Among the few spiders measured, a Portia jumping spider sees about a fifth of the detail a human sees with its big front eyes, and a net-casting spider sees less than a hundredth with its big rear middle eyes.
rows.note: One baseline, a human's 60 cycles a degree, as in the approved jumper rows: Portia 12.4, Dinopis subrufus 0.34. The ogre-faced spider of the county is a Deinopis, the same genus as Dinopis, but numbers never travel.
rows.rewrite_reason: Draft's 'a human reads about 30' makes Portia two-fifths of a human; VOICE.md's approved jumper row says a fifth. Pick one baseline.

rows.title: Pace
rows.text: Nobody has measured how fast a flicker you can see. In one crab spider, Xysticus cristatus, the front middle eyes stop seeing flicker at about 10 flashes a second, where a human stops at about 60. That figure belongs to that crab spider's eyes alone, and no one has measured it in your species.
rows.note: Left out R2 (Cupiennius salei): its quote does not clearly state a flicker limit.

rows.title: Dim light
rows.text: Some spider eyes have a tapetum, a reflective layer behind the light-sensing cells, but in spiders it is always missing from the front middle pair. In two Argiope species the light-sensing cells of the eyes become more sensitive at night, and in the nocturnal Araneus ventricosus a front middle eye also follows a daily rhythm of sensitivity. Nobody has measured how little light you need to see, or whether your other eyes have a tapetum.
rows.note: Left out the huntsman and lynx spider tapetum records and the Deinopis starlight record because the row is about most species; say if you want per-species rows.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: In the big front eyes of the jumping spider Plexippus, cells sense ultraviolet and green only, and another jumping spider, Evarcha, picked orange or blue stripes over plain surfaces of every shade of gray it was offered. In two garden spiders, Argiope bruennichi and Argiope amoena, the front eyes have three kinds of color-sensing cell, for ultraviolet, blue and green. Nobody has measured which kinds of color-sensing cell you have, or whether you can tell colors apart.
rows.note: Left out the count of gray shades and the wavelength figures, since neither has a job in the row.

rows.title: The web
rows.text: If you are a golden silk spider, you feel your prey through the silk, and a trapped insect shakes your web 5 to 30 times a second. Around the middle of your web, the shaking is ten to thirty times stronger on the side nearest the insect, which tells you which way to go. Nobody has measured this in most other spiders.
rows.note: Landolfa 1996: prey vibrations peak at 5 to 30 Hz; amplitude gradients of 20 to 30 dB (ten to thirty times) around the hub give the direction. Between the spider's own legs the gradient is about 17 dB, so the live 'on some legs' is moved to the hub.
rows.rewrite_reason: Keep live's measured golden silk spider facts, in 'you'; the draft's fishing spider sentence is about moving air, not the web.

rows.title: Hearing through silk
rows.text: If you are a bridge spider, your web moves with the air, so it works as a listening surface up to 10,000 times larger than your body. A tone played from a loudspeaker three meters away can make you crouch, stretch out or turn.
rows.note: Zhou 2022. At 68 dB the only response was crouching; at 88 dB the spiders crouched, stretched out, displayed a foreleg or turned, so 'turns toward' is softened.
rows.rewrite_reason: True and vivid; recast as 'If you are a bridge spider, you turn ...' with US 'meters'.

rows.title: Wolf spiders
rows.text: If you are a wolf spider, all your eyes but the middle pair in front are backed by a mirror layer. It reflects light back through your eyes, and it makes them shine green in a flashlight beam.
rows.note: The grate-shaped mirror layer is in the secondary eyes (all but the front middle pair), and its green eyeshine was measured in county wolf spiders such as Gladicosa pulchra and Rabidosa punctulata. No record says it helps them see movement in dim light, so that clause is left out.
rows.rewrite_reason: Recast as 'If you are a wolf spider, ...' and drop 'This picture leaves that out' (rule 3).
